steps.title: Import Component, OnInit, and HttpClient from Angular core
steps.instruction: Import Component and OnInit from '@angular/core' and HttpClient from '@angular/common/http'.
steps.hint: Use the import statement with curly braces to import multiple symbols from the same module.
steps.seedCode:
// Import Component and OnInit from '@angular/core'
// Import HttpClient from '@angular/common/http'
steps.expectedOutcome: The necessary Angular modules for creating components and making HTTP requests are imported.
successCriteria: Component and OnInit are imported from '@angular/core', and HttpClient is imported from '@angular/common/http'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported the required Angular modules for this lesson.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're importing Component and OnInit from '@angular/core' and HttpClient from '@angular/common/http'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The imports are not correct. Please import Component and OnInit from '@angular/core' and HttpClient from '@angular/common/http'.

steps.title: Create the main RaceConditionFixComponent class
steps.instruction: Create a component class named RaceConditionFixComponent that implements the OnInit interface.
steps.hint: Use the @Component decorator above the class and include the necessary imports from '@angular/core'.
steps.expectedOutcome: A component class named RaceConditionFixComponent is created with the OnInit interface implemented.
successCriteria: The RaceConditionFixComponent class is defined with @Component decorator and implements OnInit.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the RaceConditionFixComponent class with proper Angular syntax.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure your class has the @Component decorator and implements OnInit.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component class isn't quite right. Check that you've used @Component and implemented OnInit.

steps.title: Add HttpClient to the component constructor
steps.instruction: Inside the RaceConditionFixComponent class, add a constructor that accepts a parameter of type HttpClient and assigns it to a private property.
steps.hint: Use dependency injection by declaring a constructor with a parameter typed as HttpClient. Make it private so it's available throughout the component.
steps.analogousExample:
// Similar: injecting a service in a component constructor
constructor(private http: HttpClient) {}
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a constructor that properly injects HttpClient for making API calls.
successCriteria: The constructor has a private parameter of type HttpClient.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully injected HttpClient into your component. This service will be available for making HTTP requests.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure the HttpClient parameter is properly typed and marked as private.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check the constructor syntax. You need to declare a parameter with type HttpClient and make it private.

steps.title: Define state properties for user data and loading status
steps.instruction: Inside the RaceConditionFixComponent class, add two properties: userData of type any and isLoading of type boolean.
steps.hint: Define these properties directly in the class body, before the constructor.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component class now has typed properties to store API response data and track loading state.
successCriteria: The RaceConditionFixComponent class contains userData: any and isLoading: boolean properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've added the typed state properties that will hold the API response and loading status.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you've added both properties: userData (type any) and isLoading (type boolean).
steps.feedbackWrong: The component class should have two properties: userData of type any and isLoading of type boolean.

steps.title: Initialize state properties in ngOnInit
steps.instruction: Inside the ngOnInit method, set the initial values for userData and isLoading. Set userData to null and isLoading to false.
steps.hint: Use 'this' keyword to access the component's properties and assign values directly in the ngOnInit method.
steps.expectedOutcome: The ngOnInit method will initialize the component's state properties when the component loads.
successCriteria: The ngOnInit method contains assignments setting this.userData to null and this.isLoading to false.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've properly initialized the component state in ngOnInit. This ensures userData starts as null and isLoading starts as false when the component loads.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're setting both properties: userData to null and isLoading to false inside ngOnInit.
steps.feedbackWrong: The ngOnInit method should initialize both state properties. Try setting this.userData = null and this.isLoading = false inside the ngOnInit method.

steps.title: Create a method to fetch user data without race condition protection
steps.instruction: Inside the RaceConditionFixComponent class, create a method named fetchUserData that takes a userId parameter of type number and returns void. In the method body, make an HTTP GET request to 'https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users/' + userId using the HttpClient service, subscribe to the response, and update the userData property with the response data.
steps.hint: Remember to use this.http.get() for the HTTP request and handle the subscription to update the component state.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component now has a fetchUserData method that can make HTTP requests but doesn't yet handle race conditions.
successCriteria: The fetchUserData method is defined with a userId parameter, makes an HTTP GET request using HttpClient, and updates userData in the subscription.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created a method that fetches user data. Notice how this method could cause race conditions if called multiple times rapidly - we'll address this in later steps.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure your method includes: 1) A userId parameter of type number, 2) An HTTP GET request using this.http.get(), 3) A subscription that updates userData with the response.
steps.feedbackWrong: The method doesn't seem to be implemented correctly. Remember to create a method named fetchUserData that takes a userId parameter and makes an HTTP request to fetch user data.

steps.title: Add a button to trigger the problematic fetch
steps.instruction: In the component's template, add a button element with the text 'Fetch User' and bind its click event to the fetchUserData method.
steps.hint: Use Angular's event binding syntax (eventName)="methodName()" for the click event.
steps.analogousExample:
<!-- Similar: button with click handler -->
<button (click)="handleClick()">Click Me</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: A button appears in the UI that, when clicked, triggers the fetchUserData method to demonstrate the race condition issue.
successCriteria: The template contains a button element with text 'Fetch User' and its click event is bound to fetchUserData using (click)="fetchUserData()".
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added a button that triggers the problematic fetch method. This will help demonstrate the race condition issue.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure the button has the correct text 'Fetch User' and the click event is properly bound to fetchUserData using Angular's event binding syntax.
steps.feedbackWrong: The button isn't properly configured. Check that you've added a button element with the correct text and click event binding.

steps.title: Display user data and loading state in the template
steps.instruction: Inside the component's template, add conditional rendering to display user data when available and show a loading message while isLoading is true. Use Angular's *ngIf directive to conditionally render elements.
steps.hint: Use *ngIf to show different UI elements based on the isLoading and userData state properties. Remember to use property binding syntax for *ngIf.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: conditional rendering with *ngIf

Loading...

{{ userData.name }}
steps.expectedOutcome: The template will display a loading message when data is being fetched and show user data (like name or email) when available.
successCriteria: Template uses *ngIf to conditionally show loading message and user data properties based on isLoading and userData state.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added conditional rendering to display loading state and user data. This shows how state changes affect the UI in real-time.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using *ngIf correctly and displaying both loading state and user data properties.
steps.feedbackWrong: The template doesn't properly conditionally render based on isLoading and userData. Review how to use *ngIf with Angular's template syntax.

steps.title: Implement race condition fix using request cancellation
steps.instruction: Modify the fetchUserData method to store the subscription in a property and unsubscribe from any previous subscription before making a new request.
steps.hint: Create a property to hold the subscription, check if it exists before making a new request, and unsubscribe from it.
steps.expectedOutcome: The fetchUserData method will now cancel any previous HTTP request before starting a new one, preventing race conditions.
successCriteria: The component has a property to store the subscription, and fetchUserData checks for existing subscriptions and unsubscribes before making new requests.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully implemented request cancellation to prevent race conditions. The subscription property ensures only one active request at a time.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you're storing the subscription in a property and properly unsubscribing before making new requests.
steps.feedbackWrong: The race condition fix isn't fully implemented. You need to store the subscription and unsubscribe from previous requests before making new ones.

steps.title: Add a second button to demonstrate the fixed behavior
steps.instruction: Add a second button in the template that calls the fixed fetch method (you'll create this method next) and update the template to show both buttons side by side.
steps.hint: Place the new button next to the existing one, using the same button styling. Give it a descriptive label like 'Fetch User Data (Fixed)'.
steps.expectedOutcome: The template will have two buttons: one for the original fetch and one for the fixed version (to be implemented).
successCriteria: A second button is added in the template with a click handler pointing to a method that will be created later.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've added the second button. This will allow users to compare the behavior with and without race condition protection.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added a button, but make sure it's placed next to the existing one and has a descriptive label.
steps.feedbackWrong: The second button is missing or not properly placed in the template. Try adding it adjacent to the first button.
